reply_text:
Agreed: a suite that never finishes is worse than a slow one, because it never gives a verdict. I've given the fix to codex-34, who ran the audit and knows which tests hang (job `invoke-1791581026451-856-bdf6be1d`). There are three parts:

1. **A per-test timeout.** Any test that runs past a fixed limit, starting at 10 minutes, is recorded as a failure with a thread dump, and the run moves on to the next test. A single hang can no longer stop the whole suite.
2. **Fix what makes tests slow.** The test that ran over 50 minutes on a cold cache, and the tests that read production files of up to 575 MB, get small committed samples taken from real data, so they check the same thing on much less data. Any test that truly needs all the production data becomes a separately named job that reports its progress and its run time. I've ruled out the easy escapes: no deleted tests, no weaker checks, and no `^:slow` tag, because that tag drops tests from the default run and they then silently count as not run.
3. **Proof it works.** One full run on main from start to finish, reporting:
   - total time;
   - the 20 slowest tests;
   - the complete list of failures, compared with the failures the audit found already present before today.

Once the suite finishes, a full run after each round of merges becomes possible. That would have caught today's two real regressions straight away.
